title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three separate fragments.

(1) It finishes the preceding fragment (item 97) on applicability (isometric deformation) of surfaces. Euler has built pairs of mutually applicable ruled or developable-type surfaces in parametric form. He now remarks that these families are necessarily unbounded and so cannot contain a sphere. He then asserts that a closed surface admits no isometric change, citing the regular solids as the model case, so a whole sphere is rigid. Surfaces can be changed only insofar as they are not closed. A hemisphere is certainly deformable, but determining all its deformations seems 'most difficult'. This is the passage usually quoted as Euler's rigidity conjecture.

(2) Item 98, attributed to Lexell, is closed Newton–Cotes quadrature on equally spaced ordinates:
- I: trapezoid rule, h·(f0+f1)/2 over the interval AB.
- II: Simpson's rule, AC·(f0+4f1+f2)/6.
- III: Simpson's 3/8 rule, AD·(f0+3f1+3f2+f3)/8.
- IV: Boole's rule, AE·(7f0+32f1+12f2+32f3+7f4)/90.
The general weights are then characterised by moment equations. With nodes 0,1,…,N in units of the spacing and area = N·Σ w_k f(k), exactness for x^j requires Σ k^j w_k = N^j/(j+1). The right-hand sides written, 4/2, 2^4/3, 2^6/4, 2^8/5, are exactly N^j/(j+1) for N=4. So the system as written is the one for Boole's rule, though it is headed by a general AX. Checking with w = (7,32,12,32,7)/90 gives 1, 2, 16/3, 16, 256/5, all correct.

(3) Item 99, attributed to J. A. Euler, takes the logarithmic curve y = e^{-x} with subtangent 1. It asks for the excess of its infinite arc over its asymptote:
- The excess is ∫_0^∞ (√(1+e^{-2x}) − 1) dx.
- The substitution z = √(1+e^{-2x}) − 1 gives e^{-2x} = 2z+z², and the integral becomes ∫_0^{√2−1} (1+z)/(2+z) dz.
- This evaluates to √2 − 1 − ln((1+√2)/2) ≈ 0.22599.
I verified this independently via u = e^{-x}, which gives ∫_0^1 (√(1+u²) − 1)/u du.
errors: No mathematical errors. In item 98 the moment equations are headed by a general area AaXx, but their right-hand sides (4/2, 2^4/3, 2^6/4, 2^8/5) are specialised to X=E, i.e. N=4 intervals. The general form would be N^j/(j+1); this is a notational mismatch, not a mistake.
Item 99: the antiderivative is written with a constant chosen so that it vanishes at the lower end z=√2−1. The final value √2−1+ln(2/(√2+1)) is correct.

ideas.what: Closed (complete) surfaces and closed polyhedra admit no isometric deformation; non-closed pieces such as a hemisphere are flexible.
ideas.modern_name: Rigidity of closed surfaces/polyhedra (Euler's rigidity conjecture; Cauchy's theorem; Liebmann/Cohn-Vossen rigidity of the sphere/ovaloids; refuted for general polyhedra by Connelly 1977)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjecture, 1766, from this posthumous fragment), Cauchy 1813, Liebmann 1899, Cohn-Vossen 1927, Connelly 1977
ideas.where_published: Opera postuma I (1862), this fragment; widely cited in the flexible-polyhedra literature as Euler's conjecture

ideas.what: Weights for equally spaced quadrature: trapezoid, Simpson, 3/8 and Boole rules, characterised by moment equations Σ k^j w_k = N^j/(j+1).
ideas.modern_name: Closed Newton–Cotes formulas; method of undetermined coefficients / moment equations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Newton, Cotes (1722), Simpson (1743); Boole's name attached to the 5-point rule
ideas.where_published: Newton–Cotes rules are standard; Euler treats approximate quadrature in Institutiones calculi integralis (exact location unsure)

ideas.what: Excess of the arc of the logarithmic curve over its asymptote, evaluated in closed form as √2−1−ln((1+√2)/2).

deep.surprise_reason: The rigidity remark is the well-known source of 'Euler's conjecture', already cited by Connelly and others. The Newton–Cotes material and the logarithmic-curve integral are standard and correct.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image well. In item 99 the integrand after substitution is −∫dz(1+z)/(2+z) between z=√2−1 and z=0, as transcribed. The marginal asterisks beside 'Fig. 62' and 'In logarithmica' are editorial marks.
